papers.title: IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts
papers.authors: Hang Gu, Teng Wang, Zhendong Zheng, Qianyu Cheng, Wenqi Lou, Lei Gong, Xi Li, Xuehai Zhou
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.
papers.summary: Hybrid serving offloads some experts to the CPU so a single GPU can run a MoE model larger than its memory. Greedy decoding outputs from existing engines often change with where those experts sit and when they are swapped in, because the two devices use different arithmetic. A GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the CPU arithmetic, a memory layout that lets the CPU compute lossless 12-bit experts with AVX-512 dot products, and a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps the two devices without changing outputs make placement affect only speed. Across several MoE models, outputs stay bitwise identical under different expert placements, and decoding throughput averages 1.26 times the fastest baseline, peaking at 1.54 times. ==Where an expert is placed should change only how fast the run is, not the tokens produced for the same request==.

papers.title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
papers.authors: Ruijia Yang, Ruikai Li, Zeyi Wen
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning post-training for large language models has to run two workloads at once: memory-heavy rollout decoding, whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner update. Current systems either time-share every GPU between the two phases or split the devices into whole-GPU pools. Every GPU can host a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine under CUDA MPS. Optimizer state stays on the host, policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window, and a publication gate overlaps complete updates with later sampling under a dropless staleness bound, so both sides make progress on the full allocation. On H100, A800, and similar platforms, with the staleness limit set to two steps, throughput reaches 1.11 to 2.24 times that of the stronger asynchronous baseline. ==Running complementary sampling and learning on the same GPU avoids paying for a hard device split or for serial phase switching==.

papers.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
papers.authors: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
papers.abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
papers.summary: Agent serving repeatedly resends a growing execution history, and the shared KV cache quickly becomes the throughput bottleneck. Existing context-reduction methods cannot see global cache state, while runtime KV managers cannot use tool-execution information. Tracing tokens back to the tool operations that produced them shows that later operations often supersede earlier outputs and their turns, marking 64% of tokens in recorded final histories as removal candidates. Separating the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, selecting those superseded spans, and committing removals only when shared KV pressure and prefix residency make it worthwhile cuts later cache demand. Across combinations of models, harnesses, and benchmarks, throughput under the SLO is 20% to 73% higher than the strongest baseline. ==What should be evicted is history already replaced by later tool results, not whatever happens to cross a length cutoff==.

papers.title: Weave: Routing-Adaptive Runtime Warp Scheduling for MoE Megakernels
papers.authors: Ziyu Huang, Yangjie Zhou, Chenhao Zhu, Hongzhe Yan, Tianwei Qiao, Sicheng He, Zihan Liu, Peng Yu, Shulai Zhang, Xingxun Tang, Xinhao Luo, Minyi Guo, Xiu Lin, Yinghao Yu, Guodong Yang, Liping Zhang, Shixuan Sun, Qingyun Chen, Jingwen Leng
papers.abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is widely used in mainstream large language models. Under expert parallelism (EP), state-of-the-art systems fuse each MoE layer into a persistent megakernel for high performance. By the nature of EP, each GPU's communication and computation volumes vary with the routing result. However, prior work either fixes how GPU resources are divided between communication and computation at compile time (e.g., MegaMoE), or adapts to runtime dynamism only at coarse-grained SM granularity (e.g., mKernel), dedicating whole SMs to communication and leaving their Tensor Cores idle. At the finer warp granularity within each SM, static warp schedules can neither match routing-dependent loads nor prevent warps from idling while waiting for inputs or after finishing their assigned work. Therefore, we propose Weave, an MoE megakernel with three key designs. First, a spatial schedule allocates resources between communication and computation at both SM and warp granularities to match each GPU's load. Second, a temporal schedule switches warp roles as execution progresses, enlisting all warps at the start and end of a layer and selectively handing output scatter to idle communication warps. Third, a fused cost model jointly selects both schedules per GPU at launch from runtime routing statistics. Across all evaluated platforms, Weave outperforms the strongest baselines: under EP8 over DeepGEMM-MegaMoE, it speeds up the MoE layer by 1.30x geomean and up to 1.97x on SM103, and by 1.24x geomean and up to 1.72x on SM90; under EP16 on CDNA3, it beats the fastest official RCCL+AITER baseline by 1.44x geomean (up to 2.87x; 1.67x over vLLM).
papers.summary: Under expert parallelism, leading systems fuse each MoE layer into a persistent megakernel, but each GPU's communication and computation volumes shift with the routing result. Prior designs either fix the resource split between communication and computation at compile time, or adapt only at the granularity of whole SMs, leaving Tensor Cores idle once an SM is handed to communication. Allocating resources at both SM and warp granularity to match each GPU's load, switching warp roles as a layer runs, and jointly choosing both schedules at launch from a fused cost model and routing statistics can follow that dynamism. On SM103, the MoE layer is 1.30 times faster than the strongest DeepGEMM-MegaMoE baseline in the geometric mean, and up to 1.97 times faster. ==When routing changes, the on-device split between communication and computation should change with it, rather than keeping a compile-time partition==.

papers.title: Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding drafts candidate continuations before the target model verifies them, and its efficiency depends on whether limited drafting compute can anticipate the path the target will actually follow. That path has two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions, and the randomness of sampling. The first requires a target forward pass, but the second can be drawn before drafting and reused at verification. Combining those known draws with predictions from an existing drafter steers tree construction and asynchronous prefetching toward the continuations this sampling run will actually use. With no extra drafter training and no change to the target sampling distribution, decoding throughput rises by up to 24.6% over strong baselines, and by up to 13.7% in asynchronous prefetching. ==Sampling randomness need not be treated as unknown: fix it first, and the drafting budget can be spent on the candidates this run will use==.

papers.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
papers.abstract: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.
papers.summary: Long prompts often share a prefix, and reusing cached keys and values saves prefill work, but a cache hit makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix. Providers usually share the cache only within an account, yet under least privilege even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other prompts in that account. Isolating every request by default, while still keeping one cache across accounts, hides hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group in that request's own timing: routing uses only visible hits, and the first token is released on the schedule of a miss twin. At saturation on a session workload, the prediction mode retains 0.984 of unprotected sharing's throughput, compared with 0.945 for isolation by account; when more reuse crosses accounts, isolation by account falls to 0.802. ==Isolation need not mean giving up reuse, as long as hits that should stay hidden are concealed in the request's own timing==.

papers.title: AdaTree: Serving-Aware Adaptive Tree Construction for Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Soohyun Cha, Jungi Lee, Jaewoong Sim
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates generative inference of large language models (LLMs) by using a small draft model to propose multiple candidate tokens, which are then verified in parallel with the target model in a single decoding iteration. While the state-of-the-art method of tree-based speculative decoding helps improve generation throughput over non-speculative inference, deploying it in LLM serving systems often yields suboptimal performance due to dynamically changing serving conditions. In particular, our analysis shows that the optimal tree configuration---the one that maximizes performance---varies with two key serving conditions: request rate and per-request characteristics. Based on the analysis, we present AdaTree, a plug-in component for LLM serving systems that dynamically adapts tree configurations to varying serving conditions. AdaTree predicts model execution time and acceptance length across different tree configurations and selects the one that maximizes speculative decoding efficiency. To capture the non-linear relationship between tree configuration and model execution time, AdaTree employs decision trees as its core modeling primitive. Our evaluation shows that AdaTree consistently outperforms both chain-based and static tree-based speculative decoding across diverse serving conditions.
papers.summary: Tree-based speculative decoding can raise generation throughput for large language models, but in a live serving system the tree configuration that performs best changes with the request rate and with per-request characteristics. A fixed tree or a chain-style drafter therefore often sits at odds with current serving conditions. A plug-in component for the serving stack can predict model execution time and acceptance length under different tree configurations and then pick the one that maximizes speculative decoding efficiency, so the tree can follow the load. To capture the nonlinear relationship between tree configuration and execution time, it uses decision trees as its core modeling primitive. In the reported evaluation, it consistently outperforms both chain-based and static tree-based speculative decoding across diverse serving conditions. ==A speculative tree should not be frozen before launch; the shape itself should change with request rate and request characteristics==.

papers.title: Contention-Aware Flexible Execution for Machine Learning Workloads
papers.authors: Marco Kurzynski, Shaizeen Aga, Di Wu
papers.abstract: Concurrent kernel execution is a ubiquitous paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across both training and inference. That said, concurrency causes potential slowdown as concurrent kernels contend for limited GPU resources (cores, caches, memory bandwidth), which are shared between these kernels rather than exclusively available to one, as in isolated execution. This raises an important research question: to what extent does concurrency slow down kernel execution and how can it be mitigated. To answer this question, our work presents two studies. First, we characterize concurrent kernel execution extensively for the first time, to our knowledge. We conduct not just performance analysis of concurrent kernels but also memory behavior under concurrency on state-of-the-art AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs designed for datacenter AI, using the AMD-internal millisecond sampler. Based on the observations, we share insights on the slowdown along two dimensions (memory vs. compute bound, large vs. small kernels) to inform future optimizations. Second, we put the derived insights to use, aiming to deliver higher performance via targeted, flexible overlap of ML operators. Frameworks today make the simple decision of early-first for concurrent kernels, which is suboptimal. Noticing the opportunity that ML dataflow has inherent flexibility in which operators can be overlapped and how hardware resources can be allocated, we deduce simple heuristics to tune both overlap anchors and resource allocation for concurrent kernels to improve performance. We evaluate our proposed contention-aware flexible execution (termed CAFEML) across a variety of ML scenarios (inference decode, inference prefill, training) and demonstrate a speedup of up to 13% end-to-end with simple scheduling changes and no kernel rewrites.
papers.summary: In both training and inference, compute and communication kernels often run concurrently and then contend for the same cores, caches, and memory bandwidth, so concurrency is often slower than running each kernel alone. A characterization on datacenter AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs shows that the slowdown depends on whether the kernels are compute-bound or memory-bound, and on whether they are large or small. Frameworks today usually launch communication as early as they can, and that choice is not always best. Using the flexibility already present in the ML dataflow about which operators can overlap and how resources can be split, simple heuristics can retune overlap anchors and resource allocation without rewriting kernels. Across inference prefill, decode, and training, end-to-end speedups reach 13%, and about 5% in training. ==Communication need not start at the first opportunity; hiding it behind a compute operator that tolerates contention is often the better schedule==.

papers.title: Intent-Aware Caching for Efficient LLM Serving
papers.authors: Kazi Hasan Ibn Arif, JinYi Yoon, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Hans Vandierendonck, Deepu John, Bo Ji
papers.abstract: Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%. Code is available at https://github.com/hasanar1f/intent-aware-caching.
papers.summary: Serving systems for multi-turn chats cache the key-value states of conversation prefixes so later turns can reuse them and skip redundant prefill, but a hit depends on whether the conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Even when a follow-up comes, delays vary widely as users read, think, or write, and a later hit still needs earlier prefixes to remain in the cache. In real logs, different intents show different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Classifying requests by intent, learning lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs, and using those statistics to guide an eviction policy that follows an oracle-style rule puts that signal to work. On ShareChat, the cache hit rate reaches 34.6%, above 18.8% for the previous learning-based method and 12.2% for LRU. TTFT falls by up to 46.1% compared with LRU. ==Whether a prefix should be kept depends on how often that intent continues and how long the gap usually is, not only on whether the entry was used recently==.

papers.title: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension
papers.abstract: As datasets grow, analytical queries can take longer to run, slowing down data exploration, pipelines, and applications. For developers using DuckDB, reducing...
papers.summary: Analytical queries slow down as datasets grow, which holds back exploration, pipelines, and the applications on top of them. NVIDIA and DuckLabs released a GPU-native SQL engine as a DuckDB core extension: once it is installed and loaded, supported analytical queries can run on NVIDIA GPUs without rewriting SQL or changing schemas. DuckDB still parses and optimizes the SQL, the extension executes the resulting plans, and queries with unsupported features fall back to DuckDB's CPU engine, so existing scripts and interfaces can stay as they are. In cold-run comparisons on TPC-H-derived queries stored in Amazon S3, at scale factors up to 10 TB, a tuned two-GPU configuration was 3.25 to 5.50 times faster than the best tested CPU-based DuckDB setup. Query-time compute cost fell by as much as about 79%. At small scale a single GPU had the lower cost, while at the largest scale the tuned two-GPU setup was better on both runtime and cost. ==The familiar SQL workflow can stay in DuckDB, while supported query plans are handed to the GPU==.

scenario: Today's infrastructure track follows the execution path of model serving. In hybrid inference, whether an expert sits on the CPU or the GPU should not change the output, while reinforcement learning tries to co-locate sampling and learning on the same device. Agent serving has to drop history already superseded by later tool results under KV cache pressure, and MoE megakernels under expert parallelism need runtime warp scheduling that tracks routing. Speculative decoding splits into two lines: one fixes sampling randomness before drafting, and another adapts the draft tree to request rate and request characteristics. Prefix caches must both decide what to keep from user intent and hide hits that should not be shared in request timing. Concurrent kernels stop launching communication at the first opportunity, and analytical queries can hand DuckDB plans to the GPU. Overall, today's concern is filling cache, scheduling, and overlap without changing correct results.
